"Literature" said Mr. Howells, in an article that raised hubbub in England, "has become finer art in our day than it was with Dickens and Thackeray." The same may be said of burglary. It is to be regretted that the good name of the profession of housebreaking has suffered considerably in the estimation of all persons whose opinion is worth having because of certain accompanying acts that appeared to border on violence. Rightly or wrongly, a kind of odium attached itself to that arduous calling to such an extent that thoughtful parents hesitated about advising their sons to enter on an undertaking that has been looked upon as tolerably lucrative. There is no other profession that offers such advantages in the way of collecting valuable bric-a-brac and articles of doubted usefulness as the profession of burglary. This of itself would make the business one congenial to the cultivated mind; yet, strange as it may appear, it is stated on good authority that burglars are not admitted into the best society in Boston or New York unless they come in by the usual business entrance of an unlocked door or pried-open window.

Thus many of our best young men are deferred from entering a profession which affords tremendous advantages to the skillful and ingenious, simply because of the social drawbacks that such a choice of occupation involves. It may be said that the observation, disclosures and the personal danger attendant on diligent prosecution of this industry has much to do with its neglect. It is held, for instance, that the law affords equal—and somewhat similar—opportunities, and that the law is a profession that can be followed by daylight, and that the risk of encountering stray particles of lead is not so great as in the kindred pursuit of burglary. Still, lawyers are under no social ban, and so, until recently, law has been preferred to burglary.

The reason for the ill-odor of burglary is not far to seek. Burglars have been too lax in the observance of those little acts of politeness and courtesy that so largely tend to soften human intercourse. The new school of burglary will do much to change this order of things. At present this improved method is being tried with great success in Milwaukee. The case of Mr. Raw has already been referred to in these columns, and since then the telegraph brings the account of another burglary in the same city where the burglar maintained demeanor of the utmost politeness towards his client. He went on the principle that "in small affairs like these the expression, 'if you please,' implants a particularly gentlemanly tone," and no doubt so thought the sisters and the cousins and the aunts of the Milwaukee man whose house was being inventoried at the time. Instead of putting the muzzle of a pistol to a man's ear, and flashing a dark lantern under his nose, the burglar of the future will gently wake the man in the house and say to him:

"Excuse me, sir, for troubling you, but the fact is that I am looking for some little things here and am rather unacquainted with the lay of the house." The man being suddenly awakened may so far forget himself as to make remarks that in cooler moments he would regret, but these the polished burglar will take no notice of. "Excuse my seeming inquisitiveness," he will remark, blandly, "but would you be so kind as to inform me where you keep your cash."

Thus the necessary business pertaining to a visit of this kind can be transacted with decorum and pleasure by both parties.

It is not too much to hope that in the near future the occupation of burglary may be so systematized that every burglar will have a certain number of clients and that the politest burglar will have the greatest number. By strict attention to business and by respectful treatment a burglar may amass a large amount of wealth. As he rolls past in his carriage admiring friends will say, "There goes DeWinton, who has a burglary monopoly on some of the finest houses on Woodward avenue."

The system may be extended so that one burglar will have the profession's etiquette not to encroach on another's territory. If by mistake he enters a house out of his bailiwick, the proprietor will merely say: "Beg your pardon, but DeWinton does all the burglary," and the intruder, with profuse apologies, will at once withdraw.

The effect of the new school of burglary on the profession in general ought to be very great, and it is much, to the credit of a small Western town like Milwaukee, that the ethics of this important branch of industry should have been first put into practice.

Detroit Free Press.

STAFFORD, OHIO. January 20, 1885.

Local SPIRIT: It was our pleasant lot to attend a Christmas entertainment in the M. E. Church in this place on Christmas eve, and the occasion was one of manifest enjoyment to ALL. The program was an excellent one, well arranged and replete with fine selections of music and recitations. It would require too much time and space to attempt to give full description or to name all the performances, but will simply say that all did well; and indeed few of the recitations by the little girls were so well spoken that we have seen professional Elocutionists fail to render them as well. "The Old Methodist Woman" and "Mrs. Bruce's Lecture to Jeremiah" were heartily spoken and acted and ELECTED rounds OF applause. Another prime feature of the evening's entertainment was the Jubilee singing by "the boys." Such songs as "Camp in the Wilderness," "Listening to the Night," "Golden Slippers," &c., were SUNG by the colored boys in the old plantation style and with all the earnestness and feeling peculiar TO their race.

The performance ended with Letter from Santa Claus. After the reading of which he made his appearance, his back bent with the weight of years, his beard whitened with the snow of ages. He carried two huge baskets filled with SACKS of candy, and is bounded about scattering the candy among the children. One could scarcely believe him old, and once we peeped under the broad brim of his slouched hat, and really his mustache was not colored as well like his beard; we verily believe there was not gray hair in it.

Christmas night we were again entertained in EXCELLENT style but quite differently. This time we gratified the desires OF the "inner man" by partaking OF a splendid supper given at the residence of Mr. L. B. Day by Mrs. Rose Hughes and MRS. John Gaskell. Every one present seemed to have come for the purpose of having a good time, and good time we had. George lost his tobacco; Ross caught the wrong girl, but he was blindfolded and couldn't help IT; Jane lost her money; Eaton ate too many oysters for comfort, and many other little mishaps occurred, but on the whole it was a good time and every one went away feeling it was "good to have been there."

Oh, yes! Christmas day we visited the oil well, about two miles west OF town, and found them hard at work drilling. Having made a start of 81 feet in the direction OF oil, with the best machinery that can be had, and experienced workmen, it will not be long until the problem will be solved, and we hope, and indeed trust, that success will crown the efforts OF the enterprising men who have undertaken so much for the good of themselves and the county generally.

It is said that the ostrich is able to defend itself against the most ferocious beasts of the desert, and that the only foe it really dreads is man. Thus in the absence of the wings with which to fly they have been given a powerful weapon with which to protect themselves on land. What wonderful Creator!


The rhea is the ostrich of South America, though only half the size of its African cousin, still it is a very handsome bird and of fair size. The wings are small, but abundantly furnished with long, flexible soft feathers which spread like a snowy sail as it runs. The rheas are very pretty and very funny birds. They have a very curious habit of drawing in their necks, shaking out their long wing feathers, and saluting each other as if they were overcome with joy, and then dashing about in a headlong frolic, and running blindly against a fence, or bush, much to their discontinue.


The cassowary, found in the Malaccas, belongs to the ostrich family. They are easily tamed, and soon became very much attached to their owners. They are exceedingly mischievous, and, like all their species, great thieves—always feeling privileged to help themselves.


An English naturalist once owned a pair of these birds which were altogether too familiar upon his premises. He tells of them that no sooner would his cuffs be starched and hung out on the line than one of these birds would step up, and before any one could stop it swallow them instantly.


At another time he had a carpenter at work about the yard, who came rushing into his study in great alarm, exclaiming: "Doctor! oh, doctor! come quick, one of those birds of yours has been and swallowed my oil stone. It'll kill the creature sure if you don't give him something!"


"Oh, it's just like him, Patrick," the doctor coolly replied. "He'll take your hammer and chisel next; look out!"


The carpenter went back to his work, greatly disturbed, nor would he go on till the bird was placed in confinement; and then even he could not get over his solicitude for its welfare, to say nothing of the loss of his favorite stone.

The salutary virtues of a ring, independent of the enchantments and occult powers granted to it in olden times, are strikingly exemplified in the following anecdote: In the Histories et Paraboles of Father Bonaventure Girandeau (edit. 1813) is the story of a rich man, whose remorse for an ill-spent life led him to Rome to beseech the pope to convert him. The pope suggested various penances that he should undergo, but none seemed to meet his case; fasting was detrimental to his health; he had no time to read or pray; to undertake pilgrimage would interrupt his worldly affairs.—in fact, to every recommendation of the pope he had some excuse for not carrying it out. The pope heard him patiently, and on his leaving gave him a gold ring, on which was the inscription, "Memento mori"—Remember you must die—and told him that he should always wear the ring and read the inscription at least once a day. The rich man retired, congratulating himself on having so light a task imposed upon him, but, in a short time the words fell and deeper on his mind, and he said to himself "As I must die, what else have I in the world to prepare myself for it? Why regard my health that death must destroy, or think of riches that will pass away?" The conclusion of these thoughts led to his pursuing a life of rigorous self-denial and doing worthy actions, which made him beloved by all to his dying day.

In one of Hawthorne's American notes, he relates a singular incident that befell his friend, Dr. Harris, while junior at college. Being in want of money to purchase shirts and other necessaries, and not knowing how to obtain it, he set out on a walk from Cambridge to Boston. On the way he cut a stick, and after walking a short distance perceived that something had become attached to the end of it. This proved to be a gold ring, bearing the motto, "God speed thee, friend"—aal encouragement to persevere in his effort for improvement and a salutary assistance to him.

Rings, as we know, in former times were sometimes officially used in the conveyance of property, and were legally recognized as part and parcel of such transfers. In the eighteenth year of Queen Elizabeth's reign Sir Francis Englefeld settled his manor and estate at Englefeld, in Berkshire, on Francis, his nephew, with power, notwithstanding, of revoking his grant "if he during his natural life, should deliver or tender to his nephew a gold ring" with intent, says Burke, "to make void the uses of his said settlement." Various disputes and points of law arose (the manors, lands and vast possessions having been forfeited to the queen in the twenty sixth year of her reign whether the said manor and estate belonged to the queen." In order to settle the dispute on hand Elizabeth, in the ensuing session, had a special act passed establishing the forfeiture of Englefeld to herself, her heirs, and assigns, and backed by the enactment, she came upon the scene, tendered a gold ring to Sir Francis, and seized and confiscated his said manor and estate and many other possessions.

By the ingenious, if not cunning device, by which Queen Elizabeth confiscated his estates of the Englefelds, this ancient family was stripped of an inheritance in which they had flourished for 750 years. The queen's love for jewelry was unbounded, and her wily courtiers availed themselves of this passion by giving her numerous jewels as New Year presents; but among the costly rings, in which she took especial delight, none could bring her such good fortune, however equivocally employed, as the gold ring that turned the fortunes of the Englefields. — All the Year Round.

PROFESSOR WAYLAND'S LECTURE


Parliament Disraeli-Gladstone.


In accordance with the desire of a number of subscribers published in full the remarks of Professor Wayland upon England's two great statesmen.


The lecture was delivered at the Y. M. C. A. Hall and was attended by a large audience who listened with the keenest attention and the greatest pleasure.


The lecturer commenced by supposing the audience were strangers in London. DESTROYERS of hearing debate. He sketched the three methods by which admittance could be gained. The number of people who could be accommodated with seats in the Speaker's gallery, and the strangers gallery, was extremely limited; the number of tickets issued was large, and those who entered by members' tickets had to take the chance of being in the next sixty. The method of entrance having been described, the speaker next proceeded to give a picture of the House. It is an oblong chamber, at one end the Speaker's chair, at the opposite end the bar of the House, within which none but members may pass. On the floor of the House benches for the members are arranged parallel with the sides of the building with a broad passageway from the bar to the Speaker's table. Another narrow passage called the gangway crosses the first midway thus dividing the seats into four groups.


The front bench to the right of the Speaker is occupied by the Ministers for the time being, who are members of the House. On the corresponding bench to the Speaker's left are the ex-ministers or Chiefs of the Opposition. Beyond these, no member has any vested right to any particular seat, though by courtesy few of the seniors or more distinguished members are allowed to occupy the same place uninterruptedly. The Irish members, the extreme radicals and juniors generally sat on that side of the cross passage farthest from the Speaker, or in the language of the House, below the gangway.


There are no desks or facilities for writing, it is all hall of debate, and no member has a chance of being listened to if he attempted to read from manuscript or even to too freely use notes, though published documents, statistical or other, may be consulted. The lecturer once saw Mr. Gladstone make few notes on the back of an envelope taken from his pocket, and this was all the written material he had in making a speech of over two hours duration in reply to a formidable indictment of his policy. He then told of the Speaker's entrance in regular procession, and the policemen enforcing hats of strangers—all strangers—to uncover as they passed.

The prerogatives of the House were touched on, and it was shown that since 1707 no Sovereign of England had dared to refuse the loyal assent to a bill. The peculiar Norman French phraseology is still kept, assent being "with assent" and dissent by "dissent with assent or is regrarissim."


Parliamentary speaking was then touched on and the awkwardness of style alluded to. The lecturer however said there was no lack of eloquence. The manner of some of the principal speakers was briefly described, and then the Professor read the following biographical sketches which struck all hearers as being very happily put together.


DISRAELI.


Disraeli was born in London Dec 9, 1830, and after several unsuccessful attempts he entered Parliament in 1847, at the age of 17. He was already well known in society by his writings, Vivian Grey was written when he was 18. By his eccentricities of dress and demeanor and by his convex satire, all these peculiarities he imported into the House of Commons. His first attempt at speaking was an admitted and amusing failure. It was impossible to continue in the face of the shouts of laughter and ironical cheers with which he was received. His brief and indignant protest ended with these words: "Laugh down, the halls of justice shall hear me." During this session, several times, and during subsequent sessions frequently, his voice was heard in the House on any and all subjects and on all sides. He neither had nor showed any political convictions. Shortly before entering Parliament he wrote to a friend that his forte was sedition, and many of his published utterances were those of an advanced liberal. He had not long been in Parliament before became well known that he was ready to accept office under Sir Robert Peel, the leader of the Tory party. Cool, calculating, self-contained, without passion, without convictions, without conscience, adroit, ambitious and audacious and long-headed far beyond his years, he was waiting his opportunities, in his own words: "The opportunity in popular assembly has sometimes more success than the weightiest efforts of research and reason."


The eagerly awaited opportunity came at last. The rapidity with which it was seized and its controlling effect upon Disraeli's political career justify more extended allusion to the incident; it will be as brief as possible.


Sir Robert Peel had for several years been coming gradually to the conclusion that the corn laws, imposing heavy duties on foodstuffs, were unjust and oppressive and that the injustice thereof bore with increasing weight upon the laboring classes. For some time he favored a system of attic and steady reduction as the wisest policy, but the potato famine in Ireland made the alternative repeal or starvation. Peel was not the man to hesitate for a moment. He saw his duty to the country, the politician in the patriot. His very first speech at the opening of the session of 1846 was practically a proclamation of his conversion to the doctrine of free trade. When he closed, the Tory squires sat literally speechless with amazement. They were dazed. Their great leader had turned his back on all they held dear. What should they do? Whom should they follow? There was even the possibility that, wanting new guide, they might obey their better instincts and stand by their old chief.


At this precise instant, Disraeli spoke to his feet and, on the spur of the moment, poured out a torrent of carefully prepared personal abuse of the Prime Minister. It was very clever, very malignant, intensely savage, and, to those who had not taken his measure, seemed to be sincere. At all events, it was admirably adapted to accomplish its object and it succeeded to a charm. He had given voice to the indignation of the old fox-hunting squires at what, he taught them to believe, was an act of cold-blooded treachery. He had lifted them to the level of a betrayed but resolute party, with diminished but undivided ranks. Perhaps no single speech has ever had such permanent political results. The gratitude of the Tories knew no bounds. Henceforth he was their chosen champion, as he intended and desired to be. Till the day of his death, they followed his leadership with unquestioning obedience and fidelity that never wavered. Their loyalty even survived his death of 1868 when the extraordinary spectacle was presented of a conservative government accepting, advocating and passing a reform bill more radical than the previous liberal Ministry had dared to propose, or John Bright had dreamed of as possible.


Three leading members of his Cabinet had deserted him; success meant the unconditional surrender of all the positions which the Tories had maintained with reference to the extension of the right of suffrage, and yet Disraeli persevered and carried his party with him.


It was his second great victory, won by audacity, nerve, presence of mind, pluck and an adroitness of political management falling little short of genius. And the triumph purely personal. The great bulk of the party stood by him, not because they approved the measure, but because they believed in him. There was no one to take his place. It was Disraeli or defeat. They could not afford to change front on all the great questions of the day than to lose his leadership. Parliamentary history has perhaps never witnessed so perfect subjugation of the will of many to the will of one. It was virtually partnership, by the terms of which he was to furnish the brains and they were to furnish the vote. It proved to be a partnership for life.


The elimination of this eventful career—like a chapter out of Arabian Nights—or the plot of one of his own novels, was reached in the summer of 1880, when he made his triumphal entry into London, on his return from the Berlin Congress as Earl Beaconsfield and England's representative. He had hob-nobbed with Emperors and crossed swords with Bismarck. He had secured terms apparently flattering to his country. To all, securing his long policy had been vindicated; he was the idol of the populace and was supported by every morning newspaper in London but one.


Two years elapsed and brought a change. Seen in the sunlight of a sound public judgment, the brilliant foreign policy meant few useless wars with weaker nations and the boosted diplomacy of Egypt and of Cyprus. The glamour gone. Men had been behind the stage, and had found the gold to be brass, and the diamonds paste.


The Establishment absolute and entire. Parliament was dissolved in the spring of 1880. The new election brought in Mr. Gladstone with a majority of 120 at his back. His inheritance was a depleted treasury, hostile relations with several foreign powers, and not few burning questions of domestic policy clamoring for adjustment. A few months later his place in the House of Lords was vacant forever and the title of Beaconsfield disappeared from the Peerage of England. Like the shadows, so depart.

He modified that statement by showing that large amounts of silver certificates were outstanding. But the press of the country has taken up the FIRST statement, leaving out all the questions, and parade it before the country as conclusive evidence that too much silver has already been coined, and that all of it is an incumbrance except about $50,000,000. They utterly ignore the fact which the official reports show that at the close of the last fiscal year, June 30, 1885, out of a total coinage of $203,000,000, $140,000,000 in round numbers was in active circulation in the form of silver certificates, in addition to the coin in the hands of the people, of which certificates $81,550,900 was paid to the Government for customs dues during the last fiscal year at the port of New York alone more than was paid in gold and gold certificates combined. The Concert and Drama at Norway Hall Wednesday evening, was a success in every respect, good audience was present, over 800 tickets being sold. The singing was splendid and the parts in the drama were well taken. Everyone was much pleased with the entertainment. Mrs. H. L. Horne presided at the piano. "Roses and Lilies," a duet solo by Arthur Norseworthy with Mrs. Grace Hayden at the piano, took the house by storm and was encored. "Young hearts," by Mrs. Kimball and Mrs. Pike, touched the sympathies of the audience, and the last selection, "Trust her not" from Suds, by George and H. L. Horne, Mrs. Kimball and Mrs. Pike, was sung in the very best manner of the quartette. George Cummings has just had a double runner made for him for over $50. It is a beauty and a swift running sled.

The village schools began Jan. 5, with the same teachers as last term.

The officers elected of Norway Grange are as follows: W. Mullett, Master; A. Cox, Overseer; W. A. Tracy, Lecturer; H. L. Ornari, Secretary; J. J. Rove, Treas. There will be a Grange meeting and installation of officers next week.

Dr. Evans was run into the other day, and had a bone of the hand or wrist dislocated.

George Cleaves, formerly of Bridgton, is the acknowledged champion here at checkers.

Aaron Paige has a fast horse. A. N. Williamson has a sharp trot in our streets, the other evening. The latter seemed to have the faster horse.

Swan and Rowe are doing good business. They traded horse with Lowell N. Tarksy Ridge a short time ago, and now have an excellent one for the road.

Some of our physicians want a more stringent law against "quacks" passed at this session of the Legislature.

ARTICLE. W.T., Feb. 20, 1885.
To the Hon. Mayor and Common Co-
UNCILMEN: Your Committee on
sewers and Drainage, to whom was re-
ferred the communication of the City
Surveyor, in relation to needed drainage
at the intersection of Mill, Terrace and
Fourth streets, would respectfully
report that they have examined the
premises and find the condition in that
vicinity substantially as reported by the
City Surveyor.

We hoped the surface
water complained of will no longer
render travel dangerous by its encroach-
ments. But with the subsistence
of this evil, other and graver consider-
ations are likely to appear, demanding
better drainage for the basin having its
outlet near the intersection of these
streets. Sanitary considerations force
themselves upon us at this time with
more than ordinary urgency. We re-
gard the last monthly report of our City
Health Officer, Dr. Weed, as timely
warning that our city should be placed
in better sanitary condition. It is un-
wise to delay preparation for an epi-
demic until it is actually upon us. The
alarm has been sounded all over our
country, and especially along our sea-
board have the authorities of late been
more than usually active in the enforce-
ment of such sanitary regulations as
shall promote the public health and
ward off, if possible, the much dreaded
epidemic of Asiatic cholera with which
we are threatened in the near future.
Should it appear on our coast, as pre-
dicted, during the approaching summer,
it requires no prophetic vision to see,
this far in advance, that our city stands
upon a laundering volcano which in its
eruption must swallow up untold num-
bers of our population. But it is not
necessary for us to turn alarmists for
the purpose of frightening our people
into ordinary diligence. We have but
to exercise limited degree of our au-
thority to secure the desired result. The
power resides in this body, and parallel
with it is our responsibility for the use
or abuse of this power.

It may be urged that there exist no
real grounds for increased vigilance at
this time but can it be denied that we
have a filthy city? We should blush to
have the Health Officer of any respect-
able clean city visit some of these
rank smelling places now tolerated
in our city. It is not desirable, and
perhaps not necessary, to state the
whole truth in relation to this sub-
ject, but we think the time has ar-
rived when it becomes our imperative
duty to enforce, through our police,
every sanitary regulation bearing upon
individual property holders; and in order
to share with them, in some meas-
ure, the hardship which this implies, the
city should do its full duty in providing
facilities therefor. To this end, and in
view of the foregoing, we would re-
spectfully recommend as follows:
First—that the Street Commissioner
be directed to construct a suitable box
drain across James street, at the east
side of Fifth, so to convey the stag-
nant water now collected on Mr. Kin-
ney's lot into the gulch across James
street.

Second—that he be directed to con-
struct a suitable box drain from the
alley between Front and Second streets,
on Pike, so to drain into the sewer at
Pike and Union streets.

Third—that the City Surveyor assist
in this construction and furnish the
necessary information to secure proper
grades, etc.

Fourth—that the Chief of Police be
directed to use the police force, under
the direction of the Health Officer, to
discover and promptly abate nuisances.

Fifth—that the accompanying esti-
mate and map of proposed sewer at the
intersection of Mill, Terrace and Fourth
streets be referred to the Committee on
Streets and Street Improvements for
examination and recommendations.
W. V. RUSHMERE.
H. L. FELIX.

The painstaking author of this detailed narrative had the advantage of a picturesque and not too familiar subject, and he was able, by fresh researches among state and family archives to throw upon it some new light. The period covered in his work, from about 1550 to 1672, fills one of the most impressive chapters in the history of the United Provinces. The young republic had recovered rapidly from the disasters of the war of independence. Its commerce had made the round of the globe. Its colonies and trading posts flourished on the most distant. The wealth of Asia, whose mysteries were still but half revealed, flowed into its harbours. Its merchants were becoming the most powerful personages of their time. The Dutch East India Company maintained an absolute monopoly of the splendid trade of Japan and although they purchased this privilege at the cost of the basest acts of apostasy ever known, denying the name of Christ at the arrival of every cargo and lending their forces to the Government for the massacre of Christian converts, yet the profit on the trade was at least one hundred and fifty per cent—and perhaps the vehemence of the theological quarrels at home made amends for excessive liberality in the Indies. The commerce with America employed 800 vessels. Dutch ships became the carriers for all Europe. The youngest of nations was the greatest maritime power in the world. When the Dutch fleets engaged those of England the issue was for long time doubtful. Van Tromp swept the English Channel and towed broom to his masthead as a mark of derision and defiance. De Ruyter sailed up the Thames and the Medway, destroyed men in war under the fortifications of Chatham and spread panic in London. The United Provinces were studded with handsome and thriving cities between which stretched highly cultivated and blooming country. If the population under the influence of material comfort had lost some of those sturdy qualities which illustrated the heroic struggle against Spain, they nevertheless presented an attractive picture of thrifty responsibility. The life of the towns which Mr. Pontalis sketches agreeably in his introductory chapter was active and not un-elegant. Arts, sciences and letters had blossomed suddenly in the sunshine of prosperity and freedom, and the Dutch burgher was well able to hold his own in polite intercourse with any society. Moderation, however, was the fashion in personal expenditures, and domestic decorum reflected the national prudence and sobriety.

The Government of the United Provinces was a complicated organization, republican in form, but by no means democratic in spirit. The unit of authority was the town-council, composed of deputies of the trading class, for the most part self-perpetuating, although in few places the citizens had the right of voting. The town-councils appointed deputies to the provincial States, and these in turn sent representatives to the States-General; yet the authority of the States-General was in fact inferior to that of the provincial assemblies. An executive head called the Stadtholder, was chosen by the States of each of the seven provinces. In consequence of the services of the House of Orange, the war of independence had thus far directed the energies of the assemblies toward the head of that family, so that the Stadtholdership, not merely of one province, but of five or six of the seven, had become practically hereditary with the Princes of Orange. To this office was joined the supreme military and naval command. Thus the Government might be said to consist of a powerful hereditary princedom, checked by trade guilds and burgomasters. It offered extraordinary opportunities for intrigue and dissension, and although it had served the nation well in the money-making years of peace, it was too loose a confederation for the strain of foreign war; at the middle of the seventeenth century the Stadtholder of the provinces was William II, grandson of William the Silent and father of that William who became King of England. The Stadtholder of the remainder was his cousin and close ally, William III, had married the Princess Mary of England, daughter of Charles I, and had entered into a negotiation with Louis XIV for an offensive alliance with France against the Spanish Netherlands, in return for which Louis was to aid Charles in his struggle against the Parliament. But the United Provinces were resolute for peace and reduction of their army. William attempted

he died. Then the States of Holland took the lead in a movement to abolish the Stadtholdership. The others might do as they pleased within their own territory, but Holland had determined to leave the office vacant. Holland, too, the richest and most important of the provinces, would not consent to a renewal of the appointments of admiral and captain-general. The person to whom the three executive posts would naturally fall was the infant son of William II, born few days after his father's death. The action of Holland, therefore, which the other States were compelled, if not in all cases to follow, at least to respect, was primarily the exclusion of the House of Orange from an authority which seemed inconsistent with the perpetuity of the republic. But it was something more than that. There being no longer any central power, Holland became inevitably the controlling force in the confederation, and every year her preponderance grew more marked. Having deposed the Stadtholder, she practically took his place. Her Grand Pensionary, who was at once the president of the assembly and the principal administrative functionary, was appointed by the States of the provincial assembly, for five years, but was perpetually re-eligible. He was soon recognized under the new order of things as the true head of the confederation. The foreign affairs of the republic were in his hands and his authority was generally admitted by ambassadors.

To this anomalous position John De Witt was chosen in 1653 at the age of twenty-eight and he was continued in office by three re-elections until his death. His personal traits are not wildly illustrated in the pages of the work of Mr. Pontalis, but he seems to have been a man of some engaging qualities and many stalwart virtues. He showed a splendid integrity in an age when corruption, although not more common than it is now, was more respectable. His patriotism was pure and ardent, though narrow in its scope. His attachment to republican institutions was unconquerable. His courage reached an heroic grandeur and persistence. He was naughty in his manners, but amiable in his domestic relations and what we are allowed to see of him.

CITY OF MEXICO, Sept. 17.—President Diaz's message to congress is a long document, and has excited unusual interest in commercial, banking and railway circles. The comments are made on operations of the new customs tariff, nor is the banking situation discussed, being probably reserved for later consideration. The prediction was made by railway and steamship interests that the renewal of subsidies would be recommended, but it is shown to have no foundation, and railway men are disappointed as no reference to the matter in his message opens by stating the attitude assumed by Mexico when President Barrios, of Guatemala, to attest the consolidation of five Central American republics by force, has merited the approbation, not only of a great majority of Mexican people, but of other nations interested in seeing that the ancient right of conquest should not prevail. The death of Barrios and the revocation of his decree put an end to the war and the difficulties that caused it. The relations now between Guatemala and Mexico are those of sincere friendship and the new Guatemala minister acceptable to the Mexican good will soon arrive here. The President proposes the establishment of a mixed tribunal to settle claims of Mexican citizens against Guatemala. Relations with the United States continue to do most cordial. The return of the Democratic party to power, after nearly a quarter of century of Republican rule, had brought with it no interruption of the friendly relations between the two Nations. The President recommends that Senate ratify at once the postal and extradition treaties negotiated with the United States, as well as the additional article of reciprocity treaty by which article eight is prolonged in force until March 1886. He also recommends appreciation of the treaty concluded in the city of Washington, establishing certain rules of interpretation concerning article of the treaty of limits of 1858, so as to prevent difficulties on account of continually recurring deviations of the course of the Rio Grande river. A treaty of friendship and commerce has been concluded with Sweden and Norway. With all other powers Mexico continues on friendly relations, seeking mutual development of trade. Harmony in Federal and State governments is complete, and peace has been assured in the new territory of Chiapas. The government is giving attention to improvement in the mail service and telegraph lines, availing itself of stipulations in railway concessions, empowering the government to use poles for its wires. The condition of the treasury has prevented continuation of the work on the Tehuantepec road, but conservation of the completed work thereon has been attended to. Various contracts have been made for the colonization of public lands and for the exportation of products of the country. Useful plants and seeds have been distributed in agricultural sections, and special study is being given to the accumulation of mining statistics. The most important part of the message refers to financial matters. The president says that last spring he informed Congress of the pressing difficulties of the financial situation. Those difficulties increased rapidly until they came to a crisis, about the termination of the fiscal year, and neither the pursuance of measures of economy, nor the vigorous enforcement of honesty in the collection of taxes served to make the situation any better. The most radical remedies were requisite, on account of the enormous deficit and excess of appropriations over resources. The obligation of creditors to the nation, and their right to demand payment were not to be disputed, but the executive had at the same time the important obligation to provide for the maintenance of the government. Finding himself so seriously embarrassed the president decided to seek solution of the difficulty in the inspirations of patriotism and in the advice of his official councillors. It was deemed best not to add to the existing difficulties, but rather reduce expenses and to postpone payment of all those expenses not absolutely necessary to the administration of the government. Recourse was had to a plan which recognized interior and exterior debt, and enabled the government to pay its usual expenses. Several decrees were issued on June 7, of which information was once given to the permanent congressional committee. The 20 percent clause was a proposition submitted by the nailers themselves at the district meeting held in Wheeling, March, 1854; was adopted by the meeting and then carried to the Scale Convention which met in Pittsburgh April 1854; was there advocated by the nailer delegates and adopted; was embodied in the scale submitted to the manufacturers in that year; was guarded by a nailer who was on the Conference Committee, and finally agreed to by the manufacturers.

It was after the adoption of the clause that the trouble began. The clause being in the scale it became the duty of the officers of the Amalgamated Association to see that the provisions of the same were enforced. The nailers at Bellaire refused to demand that which their own class of workmen had proposed and engrafted in the scale, and they succeeded in getting some of the nailers in Bellaire to rebel also. The disease became contagious, and by aggravation spread, ending in the greatest mistake the nailers ever made—their seceding from the Amalgamated Association, though it must be admitted that they have made heroic fight against large odds—and we hope that they will yet succeed. The opposition to the twenty percent extra by the Bellaire nailers was ably championed by their delegate at the annual convention held in Pittsburgh in the month of August following its adoption, and he was the only delegate out of seventeen nailers, who were also delegates, that opposed the adoption of a resolution looking to the enforcement of the scale in relation to steel nails.

We have no motive in stating this except to show to the world that the puddlers were not responsible for the causes that led up to the greatest blunder the nailers ever made—that of demanding an extra price for cutting steel nails and then not enforcing it when they could have got it.

In summing up the whole affair, this whole trouble could have been avoided had the 20 percent extra for cutting steel nails been enforced. It was a clause of their own begetting, and not of the puddlers', and was carefully nursed by them through all the stages and regulations necessary to its adoption. Failing to enforce it, though bantling that it has matured, threatens to turn on its parents and curse them for bringing it into existence."

From the New York Sun.


The last mail from Peru brought the details of the contract entered into by the Peruvian Government with Mr. N. J. P. Grace of the firm of W. R. Grace & Co., for the completion of the Oroya Railroad and its extension to Cerro de Pasco. The Oroya road was contracted for with Mr. Henry Meiggs in 1869. According to the agreement track was to be laid from Lima to Oroya, via 764 miles northeast of Lima, in the heart of the Andes, and only few miles from Cerro de Pasco, which contains one of the richest deposits of silver in the world. Cerro de Pasco is 14,220 feet above the sea. Mr. Meiggs began laying the tracks for this road within a few months after the signing of the contract with the Government. It was in reality a government enterprise. Mr. Meiggs was to receive $21,600,000 for the work from Callao to Oroya. When the road was completed it was to belong to the government. But the government failed to carry out its part of the contract, and the work stopped. The enterprise was resumed when President Prado took hold of the government, and Mr. Meiggs invested his immense fortune in it, and lost his investment when Peru became unable to go on with the work.


The state will continue in possession of an interest in the enterprise. Mr. Grace has purchased the control of the entire property, after careful investigation of his resources and capacity. He becomes possessor of the road through agreement with the shareholders and with the government, subject to certain conditions, which are its completion to Cerro de Pasco within seven years from the date of the contract.


The Oroya Railroad was one of the most difficult and costly engineering works ever undertaken. In 1,006 miles the ascent is 16,900. There are 65 tunnels already made, one of which, called La Gloria, is 3,300 feet in length. There are also bridges, the most important of which, the Rimac, has 150 feet high and total length of 525 feet. This is said to be the highest bridge in the world. Through La Gloria the rock was so hard that the cutting had to be done with diamond drills.


The work already done on the railroad has cost $5,500,000. The country through which it runs, per하자 as it has been, is agricultural, and products are sent down to Lima. It is extremely fertile, but the methods of labor have been an antiquated and wasteful kind. With the introduction of American agricultural machinery the wealth of the country would be more than doubled, it is said.

NEW YORK, August 23d, 1881.

A thousand men and women lingered around the tomb at 6:30 O'Clock, when the young undertaker, Stephen W. Merritt, unlocked and swung open the great iron and oaken doors to allow Patrick Creyan, of Pittsburgh to seal the great solid steel outer case which enclosed the coffin and its cedar box. Seven men from Troy descended into the tomb, and by the light of Pickwick candles held aloft by boys drove fifty six bolts of steel into the front wall of the steel case, making it absolutely airtight and waterproof. Park policemen and citizens, who had got through the lines somehow, crept down toward the weirdly lighted tomb and begged and tried to buy bits of coal from the furnace at which the bolts were heated, pieces of burnt candle, rings of rubber from the bolts and even splinters of wood in which the bolts were packed. They eagerly seized them as souvenirs. Some of the bolts were round to be imperfect and were drawn out of the steel case. The last bolt was driven at 5:43 O'Clock and then the case was fastened down in place upon the packing of plumbago, inserted beneath it to prevent possible damage to the marble slabs by reason of the great weight of the steel case. It turns the scale at 1850 pounds. The whole case was next painted with dark waterproof paint to remove the work of two vandals who had scratched their names on the case while it was on exhibition. Last of all young Mr. Merritt screwed upon the west end the screws. The screws were driven with the ebonite-handled, silver plated screwdriver with which all the screws of the coffin have been fastened. It was made expressly for the purpose and will be preserved as a memo; a silver plate inscribed General Grant.

The undertaker Merritt locked the great doors with a huge brazen key and handed it over to Police Captain Beattie. Then the police formed and marched in the faint starlight, leaving the tomb under the guard of Captain Fessenden, with the locks that cluster just above the tomb.

At midnight the desolate little knoll was deserted by all save the soldier watchers. The cross above the tomb stood out in glistening outline against the sky. The echoing tramp of the sentinel sounded faintly on the night air, and just under the bluffs overlooking the river the little guard of the Fifth Artillery had gone to sleep under its white tents. The encampment has been christened Camp Grant, in memory of the dead General. Its members fought with him at Shiloh under Captain, afterward General Terrill. The camp will remain on guard for thirty days.

Chinese Ceremonies.

NEW YORK, August 9.—The obsequies were celebrated in Chinatown in a characteristic manner. At early hour the imperial standard was hung at half mast and a bulletin was issued as follows: "General Grant, a very great war General and head man of the Americans is dead. He was a very good man; observe today, his funeral day, quietly and pay proper respect to his memory." The bulletin was read by laundryman and grocer alike and its contents made known to the community. In many of the club rooms Grant's portrait was hung in place of honor on the wall and either white and violet mourning emblems, or black and white prayer cards, put alongside or beneath.

At No. Mott street, Wong All, a strict Buddhist honored the General's memory in orthodox style. In a corner of his reception room a miniature graveyard a foot square was formed upon the floor by filling the space between the walls and two pieces of timber with fine white sand three inches deep. In the center was raised a mound; on the mound was placed a porcelain bowl of tea, and at the head a saucer of roasted duck. In the four corners funeral Joss sticks were inserted in the sand. On the wall at the head of the toy cemetery was pasted a long prayer written in blue black. Joss sticks were lighted early in the morning and replaced as rapidly as they burned out. Wong All said: "The Joss stick is for Chinese GOD and make him see the tea and meat for the spirit of the dead man so that he will enter the next world happy."

Celestial attempted to honor the dead by lighting fireworks and pyrotechnics, the same as would be done in China. To the disappointment of the small boys in the neighborhood the youth was summarily suppressed by his employers after he first had broken the silence of the street. But few Chinese used the mourning emblems of their American neighbors. Lanterns or prayers, with white or white and violet ribbons, seemed favorites everywhere.

WASHINGTON, D. C., July 9.—Additional protests are constantly being received at the Interior Department from Texas cattle men against the Kansas authorities, who prevent Texas cattle from being driven through what is known as the Cherokee strip in the Indian Territory into Kansas. It is on this point that the differences of opinion arise.


The law of May 10th, 1884, prohibits the driving from one State into another of cattle having Texas fever. Some of the distinguishing marks of caricature—the tags by which the comic artists make their victims known to the public—have been so long in use they can scarcely be traced to their inventors.

For instance, there is the familiar and extraordinary figure of our Uncle Sam. Every American acknowledges kinship with him, but very few know how he came into existence. Even some of the artists who have depicted him, year after year, in his different modes and attitudes, know nothing of his origin. After making some interpolations in regard to him, and considerable research into his genealogy, I learned that an English caricaturist created him in derision long ago. The intent was to embody all the ignorance, egotism, crudeness, pretension and assertiveness of the saucy young country in the quaint figure of the old Yankee. But there was no dignity in the tall, angular, self-satisfied old man which his creators neither meant nor saw. The people of the new country saw it, however, and took him to their hearts. They adopted the idea of the beneficent uncle, and put it into song and story. Then they accepted him as he was portrayed: thin and elongated, long-haired, hatched-faced, and wearing raiment the like of which never was seen on land or sea—striped pantaloons of an economical cut, swallow-tailed coat of most antiquated design, high hat that is a challenge to all modern headwear, and vest gaudier than a tropical bird. This became the familiar figure which in comic art represented our beloved country. The idea took definite form; it became fixed in our fancy; it was a creation destined to live and grow. Uncle Sam became a fact, a reality, part of ourselves and our history.

He was first made familiar to his people in Yankee Notions, a comic paper that flourished more than a quarter of a century ago, but has long since climbed the golden stair. Nast was the first artist to lift our revered Uncle out of ridicule and contempt, endow him with proper dignity, and make him a distinctive and honored character, though he claims no credit for it. He says he remembers him as far back as he can remember anything in the way of pictures. The other artists assert that Nast has made him what he is: kind, wise, courteous, quick-witted, sunny-spirited, dignified, lovable old man, keenly alive to everything affecting the interests of his people—in short, a gentleman.

It is interesting to see now how the character of Uncle Sam has developed with the character of his people. One realizes this by comparing some of the old portraits of him with some of the more modern. In Nast's allegorical sketches we have seen him in all the phases of his strong, spirited and noble character. He has wept with Columbia over his bier of heroes; he has held fast to the old flag when it was riddled with shot and shell; he has turned his gray head aside in humiliation when the public trusts were betrayed and honors abused; he has mourned over his slain sons as they lay in the valleys, on the hills, and by the rivers of the South. His keen wit has mercilessly punctured shams, and his big heart overlooked with sympathy whom the children of his adoption suffered. Dear, quaint, grand old Uncle Sam, nay, as kind and rugged face ever beamed upon us in love and goodwill, a man who smiles his people rejoice, and when he weeps of frowns they are sorrowful as he does.

Special TO the Indianapolis Journal.


WASHINGTON, Dec. 24—Undoubtedly there
is going to be a big fight over this Dakota ques-
tion. The citizens of that Territory have pre-
sented an argument in favor of their claim and
desire for statehood which cannot be turned
aside by mere political issue. It is true that
to divide Dakota and admit the southern half to
statehood, as proposed, will bring to the Repub-
lican ranks two senators and two or three repre-
sentatives; but it is also true that no Territory
has ever presented itself with half the popular,
or one tenth as many arguments for admission
into the Union as has Dakota. It is said by the
most able Democrats that it will be an injustice
to refuse Dakota what she has asked,
which the people will rebuke. The
most ultra partisans in the Democratic
party are growing very fierce in their denuncia-
tion of the proposition, because they fear that
there are enough men with reasonable minds in
their party to give the proposition success.

tically exasperated as to see one of his own party
seized with a fit of desire to do justice. The lit-
tle fury the subject which has taken place
before in the Senate and has attracted some at-
tention is nothing to what will occur later.

 The New Mexico Stock Grower gives the following pointers for sub jects of consideration at the spring meetings of the several stock associa- tions of that territory. Most of the suggestions are equally pertinent to Arizona:

 Endorse the National Cattle and Horse Drawers association organized at St. Louis last fall.

 Provide for a complete system of inspection, both local and at markets. It pays.

 Petition Congress not to repeal the present pre-emption, desert land and timber culture laws-the means avail able to secure honest title to our graz ing lands.

 Dispense with the six-snooter at round-ups and range work.

 Prohibit gambling in roundup par ties and while there is work to be performed.

 Provide for an ample supply of bulls on the range.

 See that the resolutions regarding over stocking and range rights are strictly adhered to.

 Thoroughly discuss the subject of separating bulls from the herd at cer- tain seasons of the year. The calf crop will be larger.

 Have the water holes kept open next winter, same as last. This saves stock.

 Recommend to the railroad con- pany the appointment of live stock agent for the territory, and avoid the confusion, delay and disappointment of last years shipping season.

 See that the committee on "invest- igation of applicants for membership looks carefully into the character and standing of each applicant before recommending his admission. Don't be afraid to vote against the admission of an undesirable person, as the effic- iency of the organization depends upon the character of the member.

 Make provision for the payment of round up captains and select good men for the positions.

 Endorse the action of the Territor- ial association in securing the enforce ment of the quarantine law.

 Each member should express him. self freely upon all subjects, and not sit like bump on log, and then go home and say, "two or three feRers run the darned thing"

 Pay promptly all offered rewards which have been justly earned, or else withdraw the rewards offered and leave your stock at the mercy of thieves.

 As body, resist any unjust valua- tion of stock property for taxation purposes. The assessors meeting at Santa Fe placed prices upon stock of all kinds far above market value, which is illegal and unjust.

 Make fair and equitable arrange mcnts whereby outfits not taking wag- ons to the round-ups will pay just proportion of the expense of feeding men and transportation of provisions, etc. This is only right and justice and the cry of stinglness should rot be raised.

 Above all things, PAY YOUR DUES AND ASSESSMENTS PROMPTLY. This prevents embarrassment of the officers of he association from lack of funds, as the assessments are only levied to meet actual expenses.

Prohibit gambling in roundup parties and while there is work to be performed.

The NEWS announced yesterday, the appointment of the schedule committee to arrange the schedule by games, and everything points to a brilliant season.

Secretary Walter R. Brown, of Atlanta, in an interview on Saturday, said: "I look for fully as much interest as in the past season, if not more. All the letters that I have received, indicate that the Southern season will be most profitable and pleasant."

"Has Atlanta signed any players yet?"

"No, but she will sign within the next thirty days, and she will get a good team. The Atlantas don't intend to let their colors trail. The American Association at its meeting in Philadelphia on Dec. granted alliance papers to the Southern League, and the agreement has been forwarded to President Proudfit, of Macon, for his signature. Under the alliance papers all the contracts with players will be protected."

"When will the season open?"

"The season will run from April to Sept. 15—five months. President Proudfit has appointed a schedule committee, which will meet at an early date and fix complete schedule of all the games to be played."

"What is the outlook for good games?"

"It is understood that the Southern league clubs will have excellent material, and will be better equipped generally than last year.
